ety.text: Latin cumlbor. English cum Learned borrowing from Latin cum.

Variant of come, attested (in the basic sense "come, move from further to nearer, arrive") since Old English. The sexual sense of come is attested since the 1650s. In this sense and spelling, attested from 1970s.

senses.d: Used in indicating a thing or person which has two or more roles, functions, or natures, or which has changed from one to another.
ex: He is too good an actor to need that sort of tomfoolery: the effect will be far better if he is a credible mining camp elder-cum-publican.
One driver-cum-fireman-cum-fitter looks after the three locomotives, [...].
Jim descends into the murky tunnel; the faint odor of cum permeates the air.
Licking a friend's cum off another friend's belly.

senses.d: To have an orgasm, to feel the sensation of an orgasm.
ex: Despite claims to the contrary, a woman can cum from anal sex alone.
Some men cum as much as 10 milliliters.
I got no sensation down there, so I don't know when I'm hard, I don't know when I cum. My wife's gotta tell me.

ety.text: From Latin sĭt, third-person singular present subjunctive of sum.

Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English cumulative From cumulate + -ive. Compare also French cumulatif, Italian cumulativo and Spanish cumulativo.

senses.d: Incorporating all current and previous data up to the present or at the time of measuring or collating.
That is formed by an accumulation of successive additions.
ex: As for knowledge which man receiveth by teaching, it is cumulative, not original.
The argument […] is in very truth not logical and single, but moral and cumulative.
cumulative conjunctions like and, both…and and as well as

senses.d: Having priority rights to receive a dividend that accrue until paid.
(of evidence, witnesses, etc.) Intended to illustrate an argument that has already been demonstrated excessively.
ex: The state wants to bring in ten blood-spatter experts to testify. Your Honor, that is cumulative testimony.
